title: School and Dido (1.13–1.16)
hook: he wept over a fictional queen and not over his own soul
tomorrow: would he have stolen those pears all by himself?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jealous baby, pale and bitter in the nursery, and a will that bends before it can speak. The line: it starts early.

A season finale ends, and the group chat fills with crying faces over a character who never existed. Augustine would understand. As a schoolboy he wept over a queen in a poem: Dido of Carthage, who dies when the hero Aeneas sails away, in Virgil's Aeneid. He loved that lesson. He hated the next one, the drill of one and one, two, two and two, four. The grown man writing to God looks back at the boy's tears and asks what they were for.
screen: `CRYING OVER SOMEONE WHO NEVER LIVED.` → `DIDO, IN VIRGIL'S POEM.` → `WHAT WERE THE TEARS FOR?`

segments.voice: His answer stings. He was made to learn the wanderings of Aeneas, he says, while forgetting his own. He wept for Dido, and never wept for himself, dying, far from God, the whole time he was reading. So: are stories that move us a distraction from the soul, or a road to it? Catholics have read this page both ways. One side leans on Augustine's own words. A few chapters on, in Carthage, he says he loved the theater, sorrows he could enjoy without having to help anyone. On this reading, feelings spent on fiction can stand in for the real thing. You cry for Dido and walk past your own life. The other side points to the Gospel itself. Jesus told stories about people who may never have lived: a man who fell among robbers, a stranger who stopped. And he ended that one, in the Douay-Rheims, "Go, and do thou in like manner." On this reading, a story is how a heart gets moved toward someone real. Notice what Augustine himself does not say. He doesn't call the poem worthless. He admits he loved it, and that he'd have been sad if it were taken away. His charge is narrower: the tears weren't the problem; where they went was.
screen: `AENEAS'S WANDERINGS, NOT HIS OWN.` · `ONE SIDE: STAGE SORROWS, NO HELP.` · `THE OTHER: JESUS TOLD STORIES TOO.` · `NOT THE TEARS, BUT WHERE THEY WENT.` · then, large: `WEEPING FOR DIDO.`

segments.voice: Put on one song that has moved you before, or recall it so clearly you can hear the opening notes. Listen to it once, all the way through, and let your attention follow where the feeling goes: toward a memory, toward a person, toward nowhere at all. Stay with whoever it brings to mind.
School and Dido. Augustine at his lessons, weeping for a queen in Virgil's poem while, he says, he shed no tears for his own soul.
